newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim apologises for scandal, banishes son.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim apologises for scandal, banishes son.

text.p: In a dramatic gesture of contrition to try to salvage his presidency, South Korea's Kim Young-sam apologised on Tuesday for a loans scandal and promised to banish a controversial son from public life.

Appearing chastened and solemn in a televised address on the fourth anniversary of his inauguration, Kim said he was in "agony and sorrow" over the scandal, sparked by dubious loans to the failed Hanbo Steel Co.
He said he was ashamed that his own son had become embroiled in the affair.
Three of Kim's closest aides have been arrested in relation to the scandal, which has rocked the nation.
"I, as the president, offer a sincere apology to the people over this incident," said white-haired Kim, eyes downcast as he read from a prepared text in the 18-minute address.
Prosecutors said banks pressured by politicians offered huge loans in return for kickbacks from Hanbo, which racked up $5.8 billion in debts before going under on January 23.
Government officials said the cabinet and senior ruling party officials would offer to resign en masse to give Kim a free hand to reshuffle his administration.
Top presidential Blue House aides also told the president they were prepared to go, one aide said.

Kim had been widely expected to apologise, to claw back support for an administration that was swept to power pledging to clean up society but which is now lurching from one corruption scandal to another.
He is constitutionally barred from another term but is eager to avoid a lame duck tag during his last year in office and wants to put a protege in the Blue House to shield him in retirement.

Kim was a model of penitence, following in a long Korean tradition of leaders appealing for understanding for their shortcomings in office. According to custom, he kept his gaze low, his voice hushed and his manner grave.
The spectacle of a once-popular president begging forgiveness drew some public sympathy, but little forgiveness.
"His speech was sincere, but it can't make up for his four years of failures," said Oh Kil-hwan, 45.
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics, which has claimed a cover-up in a prosecution enquiry, was also dissatisfied. It demanded an independent probe.
Prosecutors questioned Kim's second son, Hyun-chul, 38, last weekend about the Hanbo scandal but cleared him of wrongdoing.

Nevertheless, Kim said he would bar his son from social activities until the end of his five-year term next February. Hyun-chul later said he would resign from all posts, and media reports said he might leave the country for a spell.
A prosecution official said Hyun-chul on Tuesday withdrew legal action against opposition politicians he said defamed him in connection with the scandal.

"I have travelled a one-way road with self-restraint and abstinence in the past four years and am devastated and in despair," Kim said, referring to the anti-corruption drive he launched shortly after taking office in 1993.
"The whole nation is now swept by shocks from the Hanbo incident."
Prosecutors last week indicted 10 people including a cabinet minister, prominent politicians, top bankers and the founder of the Hanbo Group, the country's 14th biggest conglomerate.
"Whatever the reasons, all these are the consequence of my lack of virtue. It is the responsibility of myself, the president," Kim said.
Kim's humility was in striking contrast to his combative appearance on television a month ago when he assailed the political opposition.

He also apologised for the passage of a labour law in a way that recalled the tactics of his military predecessors and sparked nearly a month of strikes. The bill was rammed through parliament in a dawn session while opposition deputies slept.
"I feel sorry for worrying the public while revising the labour law late last year," he said.
Kim's reformist image has also been hurt by a hawkish stance towards North Korea and a crackdown on student protests, and he has become the least popular president in the nation's history.
Kim's popularity topped 90 percent when he launched his anti-graft campaign in 1993 but is now around 10 percent.
